Issued at 1141 PM CDT Mon Oct 26 2026

Tonight and Tomorrow:

Water vapor imagery this evening shows a busy mid-to-upper air 
pattern, with slight troughing over the western half of the CONUS 
while potent shortwaves bring precipitation and some rumbles of 
thunder across the Southern and Northern Plains in addition to the 
Intermountain West. Drilling down to the surface, the pair of 
shortwave troughs over the Great Plains are combining to overspread 
the area with scattered rainfall and cooler conditions ushered in by 
a cold front from the TX Panhandle to southeast Nebraska. The most 
impactful conditions for the short-term forecast will be in 
place tonight as warm air advection and frontogenesis remain in 
place, resulting in enough lift in the low-levels to continue 
drizzle and some lower visibilities across northeast Nebraska. 
AWOS stations and cameras in the area have shown values of 
around a mile at times, with winds out of the northwest expected
to continue overnight as temperatures dip in the upper 30s to 
40s. 

Overnight through sunrise tomorrow, a bit of life will return to the 
radar screen as the southern shortwave trough has its associated PVA 
and height falls pushing across southeast Nebraska into Iowa through 
the morning hours. Total amounts should remain modest at about half 
an inch or less, with the center of that band remaining southeast of 
Omaha and Lincoln. The entire area will feel the effects of the 
slightly cooler airmass and lingering clouds as highs top out in the 
60s despite increasing sun across northeast Nebraska. Areas near 
Interstate 80 and points south will hold onto a saturated lower 
atmosphere, with many of the CAMs hinting at some drizzle/dreary 
conditions that could linger into the evening and overnight hours, 
which is under-represented in the NBM. Those conditions would last 
through much of the night, potentially bringing lower visibility 
values and some additional dampening to the ground as temps bottom 
out in the 50s.

Wednesday and Beyond:

By Wednesday, we'll see the mid/upper pattern return to west-
southwesterly return while southerly winds arrive at the surface. 
The jet stream will be set up just to the northwest of the area, 
with slight troughing over the western half of the CONUS while a 
ribbon of warmer low-level temps and increased moisture is able
to reach through a good chunk of the Great Plains. We'll be 
right in the path of a shifting frontal zone that gets nudged 
north and south by shortwaves that dump out across the Plains 
from the southwesterly flow to the west, resulting in minor, but
daily rain chances across the region. Cooler highs from Tuesday
turn warm once again Wednesday as strong southerlies develop, 
with gusts of 25-35 mph being depicted by EPS members in a 
narrow distribution, helping highs into the 70s to near 80 
degrees at Falls City. A weak front drags through the area 
Thursday, cooling highs a bit as the main system shoots well 
north of the area. That frontal zone then lifts northward Friday
through the weekend, with highs currently slated for the 60s 
and 70s as rain and cloud cover make or break any one location's
high temperature forecast. Though models depict QPF through 
much of this period, our most meaningful slug of moisture 
develops in the WAA region of a northeastward-ejecting shortwave
from the Southern Plains to Mid-Mississippi Valley, with the 
southeastern half of the forecast area likely to see another 
0.5-1" of rainfall Friday night through Saturday.

Heading into the upcoming work week, our eyes continue to be on a 
quickly-deepening cutoff low that centers itself over Kansas Monday 
into Tuesday before ejecting northeastward, slowing down as it 
shifts eastward Wednesday and Thursday next week. It'll bring with 
it increasing winds at the surface and cooler temperatures that just 
don't get cold enough to bring in our first snowfall chances (at 
least with the most recent runs). The most likely scenario will be a 
muddy set of days that farmers may want to beat if they don't want 
to work in soggy fields, soaked by 1-2" of rain.
